title: Differentiation from first principles
examples: When do I need to use the limit definition for derivatives?
Can you show me how to differentiate a more complex function?
Is this method only for polynomial functions?

explain.say: Today we learn to find the derivative from first principles. This means using limits to find the rate of change. We start with the definition of the derivative for a function f of x. It is written as the limit of the difference quotient. This formula is f open parenthesis x plus h) minus f open parenthesis x) all divided by h as h approaches zero. This formula gives us the instantaneous rate of ch

Let us use a simple example to practice this concept. Suppose our function is f of x equals x squared. We need to find f open parenthesis x plus h) first. This gives us x plus h all squared. Remember that x plus h all squared is x squared plus two x h plus h squared.

Next we substitute these parts into the difference quotient. We calculate f open parenthesis x plus h) minus f open parenthesis x). This becomes x squared plus two x h plus h squared minus x squared. The x squared terms cancel out, leaving us with two x h plus h squared.
Now we divide this result by h. We take two x h plus h squared all divided by h. We can factor h out of the numerator and cancel it with the h in the denominator. This leaves us with two x plus h.

Finally, we take the limit as h approaches zero. We evaluate the limit of two x plus h as h approaches zero. When h goes to zero, the term h disappears. So the derivative is simply two x. This is how we prove the derivative of x squared.

faq.q: Do I always have to use this limit definition when finding a derivative?
faq.a: No you do not always have to use this method. For basic functions like x squared, we usually use the power rule. However, understanding this definition is important for proving rules.
asks: What is the definition of a derivative?
When is the limit definition necessary?

faq.q: What does 'h approaches zero' actually mean in practice?
faq.a: It means we are looking at what value the expression gets closer and closer to. We substitute zero for h only after we have simplified the expression fully. This avoids dividing by zero.
asks: How do I handle h going to zero?
What does taking a limit mean?

faq.q: If my function is more complicated, like sine of x, can I still use this method?
faq.a: Yes you can use this method for any function. However, you will need to know the limit values for trigonometric functions. It takes more algebra.
asks: Does this work for trig functions?
Is this method universal for all functions?

faq.q: Is the derivative always the same sign?
faq.a: No the derivative can be positive negative or zero. The sign tells us if the original function is increasing decreasing or stationary at that point.
asks: What does the sign of the derivative mean?

faq.q: What is the difference between the derivative and the gradient?
faq.a: They are essentially the same concept in this context. The derivative is the mathematical tool we use to find the gradient or slope of a curve at a specific point.

facts: The derivative represents the instantaneous rate of change of a function.
The difference quotient is the formula used to define the derivative using limits.
If f of x equals x squared, its derivative is two x.
When evaluating the limit, h approaches zero after algebraic simplification.

quiz.say: Find the derivative of f of x equals 3x squared minus 1 from first principles.
quiz.why: When you apply the limit definition to 3x squared minus 1, the constant term cancels out, leaving you with the derivative of 3x squared, which is 6x.

wrong.0: This mistake occurs if you incorrectly treat the derivative as just multiplying the coefficient by the power, forgetting the reduction in power.
wrong.1: This mistake suggests you are simply differentiating term by term without using the limit process.
wrong.3: This mistake happens because you only differentiate the x squared term and forget to multiply by 3.

quiz.say: If f of x equals 5x, what is the derivative using the limit definition?
quiz.why: The limit definition applied to 5x results in the terms cancelling until only the constant 5 remains, showing the rate of change of a straight line.

wrong.1: This mistake forgets that the derivative measures the rate of change, not the original function value.
wrong.2: This mistake incorrectly adds one to the result, confusing the derivative with an offset value.
wrong.3: This mistake assumes that any function involving x must have a derivative of zero, which is only true for constant functions.

quiz.say: The derivative of f of x equals x cubed is found by evaluating the limit of which expression?

options.show: f(x+h) plus f(x) divided by h
options.say: f(x+h) plus f(x) divided by h

options.show: f(x+h) minus f(x) multiplied by h
options.say: f(x+h) minus f(x) multiplied by h

quiz.why: The process always requires setting up the difference quotient, which is the difference between the function at x plus h and the function at x, all divided by h.

wrong.1: This mistake incorrectly uses addition instead of subtraction in the numerator of the difference quotient.
wrong.2: This mistake incorrectly multiplies by h instead of dividing by h in the final step.
wrong.3: This mistake forgets the essential step of dividing the difference by h before taking the limit.
